questions.question_text: A tractor is bought for $\$96\,000$ and depreciates at $22\%$ p.a. What is its salvage value after $3$ years, to the nearest cent?

options.why: This is the total depreciation $V_{0}-S$, not the salvage value asked for.
Used $(1+r)^{n}$ instead of $(1-r)^{n}$, growing the value instead of shrinking it.
Subtracted $22\%$ of $\$96\,000$ as a flat $\$21\,120$ three times, treating the loss as constant.

questions.question_text: A courier van costs $\$54\,000$ and depreciates at $30\%$ p.a. By how much has it depreciated in total after $2$ years?

options.why: This is the salvage value left, not the amount of value lost.
Subtracted $30\%$ of $\$54\,000$ as a flat $\$16\,200$ each year, treating the loss as constant.
Used $(1+r)^{n}$ and then subtracted the initial value, so the sign of $r$ was wrong.

questions.question_text: Business equipment depreciating at $25\%$ p.a. has a salvage value of $\$17\,718.75$ after $4$ years. What was its purchase price, to the nearest dollar?

options.why: Multiplied by $(1+r)^{n}$, using a growth multiplier instead of dividing by the decay multiplier.
Multiplied by $(1-r)^{n}$ instead of dividing, shrinking the value a second time.
Divided by $(1-r)$ once only, using $n=1$ instead of $n=4$.

questions.question_text: A bakery oven bought for $\$18\,000$ is worth $\$14\,580$ after $2$ years. What is the annual depreciation rate?

options.why: Divided the total loss of $\$3420$ by $\$18\,000$ and halved it, treating the loss as constant.
Gave the total percentage lost over both years instead of the rate per year.
Gave the multiplier $1-r=0.9$ as a percentage instead of the rate $r$.

questions.question_text: A forklift bought for $\$28\,000$ depreciates at $30\%$ p.a. After how many whole years is it first worth less than $\$8000$?

options.why: Stopped at $n=3$, where the value is $\$9604$ and still above $\$8000$.
Went one year past the first year in which the value drops below $\$8000$.
Used $(0.3)^{n}$ as the multiplier instead of $(0.7)^{n}$, so the value falls far too fast.
Gave the multiplier $1-r=0.75$ as a percentage instead of the rate $r$.
Divided the $\$7500$ drop by the year-$1$ value of $\$22\,500$ instead of by the purchase price.
Misread the year-$1$ value from the graph as $\$24\,000$ rather than $\$22\,500$.

questions.solution_text:
From the graph, $V_{0}=\$30\,000$ and the value after $1$ year is $\$22\,500$.
$22\,500 = 30\,000(1-r)^{1}$
$1-r=0.75$
$r=0.25$
The lathe depreciates at $25\%$ p.a.

questions.question_text: The value of a printing press is given by $14\,000(0.83)^{6}$. Which statement describes this asset?

options.text: A $\$14\,000$ press depreciating at $17\%$ p.a. for $6$ years
A $\$14\,000$ press depreciating at $83\%$ p.a. for $6$ years
options.why: Read the multiplier $0.83$ as the depreciation rate itself instead of solving $1-r=0.83$.

options.text: A $\$14\,000$ press growing in value at $17\%$ p.a. for $6$ years
options.why: Found $r=0.17$ correctly but treated $(0.83)^{6}$ as a growth factor, so the direction of the change is reversed.

options.text: A $\$14\,000$ press growing in value at $83\%$ p.a. for $6$ years
options.why: Made both slips: read $0.83$ straight off as the rate and also took the bracket to be a growth multiplier.

questions.solution_text:
$1-r=0.83$
$r=0.17$
The expression is the value of a $\$14\,000$ press depreciating at $17\%$ p.a. for $6$ years.

questions.question_text: A bus costs $\$150\,000$ and depreciates at $16\%$ p.a. How much more value does it lose during the $1$st year than during the $4$th year, to the nearest cent?

options.why: Gave the loss during the $4$th year rather than the difference between the two losses.
Assumed the same dollar amount is lost each year, which is straight-line thinking.
Used the value at the end of the $4$th year as the base, so the loss was taken one year too late.

questions.question_text: A quarry crusher depreciates at $30\%$ p.a. After how many whole years is it first worth less than one fifth of its purchase price?

options.why: Stopped at $(0.7)^{4}=0.2401$, which is still more than one fifth.
Subtracted $30\%$ of the purchase price as a flat amount each year, treating the loss as constant.
Compared the multiplier with one half instead of one fifth, stopping at $(0.7)^{2}=0.49$.

questions.solution_text:
$V_{0}(0.7)^{n}<0.2V_{0}$
$(0.7)^{n}<0.2$
$n=4$: $(0.7)^{4}=0.2401$
$n=5$: $(0.7)^{5}=0.16807$
It is first worth less than one fifth of its purchase price after $5$ years.
